newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey says still inspecting U.S. wheat cargo.
newsitem.headline: Turkey says still inspecting U.S. wheat cargo.

text.p: Turkey is still inspecting a cargo of 15,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat suspected of carrying ergot fungus, agriculture ministry officials said on Wednesday.
"The wheat is currently under inspection," a senior official said. "There is no decision whether to reject the wheat or not," he told Reuters.

The U.S. said Turkey last week rejected 15,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat imported by a private miller after Turkish inspectors found traces of ergot fungus in the shipment, which arrived at the western port of Tekirdag last week.
The U.S. stopped issuing export certificates for wheat shipments to Turkey on October 18 in response to the recent implementation of what it said was a zero-tolerance policy on wheat quality.
But Turkish officials said Turkey was not imposing zero-tolerance. "The tolerance ratio is 0.1 percent for wheat imported for food and zero for seed wheat," the official said.

Turkey has two pieces of legislation that cover inspection of imported goods. The Food Act imposes a 0.05 percent tolerance level on wheat imports, but the Farm Quarantine Act, prepared to comply with a customs union deal with the European Union (EU), imposes zero-tolerance.
Ilker Tanik, secretary general of the Turkish Millers' Association, said the U.S. wheat should be cleared without any problem according to the Food Act.
"But if the government insists on the zero-tolerance rule, there is no chance for the U.S. wheat. But we think the ministry has a misunderstanding in the Quarantine Act," he said.
"We hope the issue will be resolved soon, otherwise millers will be in a difficult situation," he said.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) said it was considering halting export licences for other commodities, including corn and soybeans if the issue was not resolved.

Grain industry analysts and U.S. agriculture officials said it was virtually impossible to guarantee a complete absence of ergot and that the allowable 0.05 percent amount was low and did not pose any health hazards.

"To my knowledge no country in the world can meet zero-tolerance requirements," a U.S. embassy official in Ankara said. He said Turkey had told the U.S. the action was part of its pledge to comply with EU import rules after entering into a customs union deal with the EU from January this year.
USDA officials said EU plant quarantine experts were now clarifying the EU position on Turkey.

"I think there is a misunderstanding (by Turkey) in the European Union requirement. We also have exports to the EU and this is the evidence that they don't have a zero-tolerance requirement," the U.S. embassy official said.
He said Turkish flour millers needed high-protein U.S. wheat to blend with the lower quality local crop to produce flour for exports to Middle East.
Tanik said two loads of U.S. wheat, each of 16,000 to 18,000 tonnes, were also awaiting inspection at Derince and Izmir.
